---
title: "The Anatomy of Embedding and Latent Spaces"
subtitle: "From Shannon's Bits to High-Dimensional Geometric Knowledge"
---

In 1948, Claude Shannon defined information as the reduction of uncertainty, measured in bits [@shannon1948mathematical]. His entropy formula turned out to be identical in form to the one Boltzmann and Gibbs had used for thermodynamic systems in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries—a resemblance Shannon himself noted, though it was Edwin T. Jaynes who, in 1957, argued that statistical mechanics is itself a form of inference. But Shannon drew a deliberate boundary: "[t]hese semantic aspects of communication are irrelevant to the engineering problem." A bit is a unit of uncertainty, not of meaning.

The **Embedding Revolution** is the complement to Shannon's syntactic theory: it represents meaning itself—or at least its statistical shadow—as continuous coordinates on high-dimensional manifolds. Fittingly, it does so using Shannon's own tools: cross-entropy and mutual information are the objectives that shape these spaces.

This chapter lays the foundation for the rest of the book. We start with why discrete, orthogonal representations hit a geometric wall, then examine how latent manifolds are built and what their geometry looks like. We close with the structural cracks in this first abstraction—cracks that motivate the refinements explored in later chapters.

## Shannon's Information Theory

Shannon measured the information of a message by its surprise: a message with probability $p$ carries $-\log_2 p$ bits. Near-certain messages ($p \approx 1$) tell us almost nothing, while rare ones ($p \approx 0$) are highly informative. The *entropy* of a source is the average of this surprisal. For a binary source that emits a one with probability $p$ and a zero with probability $1-p$, it is

$$
H_b(p) = -p \log_2 p - (1-p)\log_2(1-p),
$$

which peaks at one bit when $p = 1/2$ and vanishes when the outcome is certain. For a stream of $n$ bits that are independent and identically distributed, entropies add:

$$
H(X_1,\dots,X_n) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} H(X_i) = n\,H_b(p).
$$

Consider a faulty sensor that outputs a one with probability $p = 0.9$. Seeing a one is unsurprising, while seeing a zero is a rare event:

| $p$ | Surprisal of a one | Surprisal of a zero | Entropy $H_b(p)$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 0.50 | 1.000 bits | 1.000 bits | 1.000 bits |
| 0.90 | 0.152 bits | 3.322 bits | 0.469 bits |
| 0.99 | 0.014 bits | 6.644 bits | 0.081 bits |

: Surprisal of each outcome and entropy of a binary source. {#tbl-binary-entropy}

For $p = 0.9$ the average is $H_b(0.9) = 0.9 \times 0.152 + 0.1 \times 3.322 \approx 0.47$ bits per symbol. The zeros are individually informative, but they are so rare that the stream as a whole is highly predictable. A fair coin cannot be compressed, because every flip costs a full bit. The sensor stream can: a log of 1000 symbols can, on average, be squeezed into about 470 bits, and no lossless scheme can do better.


::: {.questions}
1. A sensor emits a one with probability $p = 0.8$ and a zero otherwise, independently at each step. Compute the surprisal of a one and of a zero, the entropy $H_b(0.8)$, and the minimum expected size, in bits, of a lossless encoding of a 10,000-symbol log. How does this compare with a fair coin?

2. A general sends one of two equally likely messages: "attack at dawn" or "attack at dusk". How many bits does each message carry according to Shannon? Now replace "attack at dusk" with the meaningless string "xqzv jwk", keeping its probability fixed. Does the entropy change, and what does this tell you about the relationship between entropy and meaning?
:::


## Shannon's Boundary Problem

Notice what the calculations above needed: the probabilities of the symbols, and nothing else. The sensor could report temperatures, heartbeats or coin flips and its entropy would be the same. Ignoring meaning was not a weakness but the source of the theory's power. Because entropy depends only on probabilities, the same mathematics applies to any source and any channel, and it became foundational across computer science: the compression behind every ZIP, JPEG and MP3, the error-correcting codes in our disks, QR codes and mobile networks, the capacity limits that govern Wi-Fi and fiber, and, through cross-entropy, the loss function that trains modern neural networks. Shannon had already laid the other foundation of computing in his 1937 master's thesis, where he showed that Boolean algebra describes switching circuits. 

However, that indifference to meaning is also the boundary of the theory. The messages "attack at dawn" and "attack at dusk" can have the same probability, and therefore exactly the same information content, yet they mean very different things. A one-bit message has the same entropy whether it says that a coin landed heads or that today is raining. For Shannon this was a feature: the engineer's job is to deliver the message faithfully through a channel, not to understand it.

His collaborator Warren Weaver made the division explicit in 1949 by splitting the communication problem into three levels: **A**, the technical problem (how accurately can symbols be transmitted?); **B**, the semantic problem (how precisely do the symbols convey the desired meaning?); and **C**, the effectiveness problem (how well does the received meaning change behavior?). Shannon solved level A. Embeddings are an attempt at level B, and alignment techniques such as RLHF and agents are arguably attempts at level C. This is a map of the whole book.

Shannon also showed, in the same 1948 paper, how far statistics alone can go. He generated English-like text by choosing each word according to how often it follows the previous one, and obtained [@shannon1948mathematical]:

> `THE HEAD AND IN FRONTAL ATTACK ON AN ENGLISH WRITER...`

Locally the text is plausible, since each word follows its predecessor with a believable frequency, yet globally it is meaningless. It is a language model in embryo: it has absorbed some of the syntax and none of the semantics. Seventy years later, the same recipe with vastly more data and a far richer notion of context produces the large language models we will meet in this book. Shannon himself was wary of the hype that success brought. In "The Bandwagon" (1956) he warned that information theory had become a fashion, and that borrowing its vocabulary for psychology, biology or linguistics did not make those fields more rigorous. Like relativity and quantum theory, it suffered the fate of successful theories: its words travelled much further than its mathematics. Yet the separation of form from meaning was not Shannon's alone: linguistics reached it independently.

::: {.questions}
1. Take a plain-text book from the Internet (for example, from Project Gutenberg) and compute the probability of each letter. What is the entropy of this distribution, and how does it compare with $\log_2 26$?

2. With the same book, compute the probability of each word. What is its entropy? Where does the difference with the letter entropy come from?

3. Finally, estimate the probability of each word given the previous $n$ words and use it to generate a random phrase. How does the result change as $n$ grows from 1 to 3?
:::

## Chomsky's Staircase: Structure Without Meaning

The same separation between the form of a message and what it means appeared in linguistics within a decade of Shannon's paper. Chomsky classified formal languages by the machine needed to recognize them, and each machine on the staircase adds one kind of memory [@chomsky1956three]. A finite automaton has no memory beyond its current state, so it recognizes the regular languages, whose patterns depend only on a bounded amount of recent history. A pushdown automaton adds a stack, a last-in first-out memory of unbounded size, which is exactly what is needed to match nested structure such as balanced parentheses (push when a bracket opens, pop when it closes), and it recognizes the context-free languages. Linear-bounded automata, which recognize the context-sensitive languages, get a working tape as long as the input, and Turing machines, at the top, get an unbounded tape. The staircase classifies sets of strings, but the same machines can carry probabilities on their transitions: a Markov chain or hidden Markov model is a probabilistic finite automaton, and a probabilistic context-free grammar is its context-free counterpart. The probabilities decide which strings are likely, not what the machine can remember, so the memory of each step stays the same.

Shannon's word-pair text comes from a bigram model, the probabilistic version of the bottom step: a Markov chain in which the previous word alone sets the probabilities of the next. Its only memory is that previous word, so it cannot even remember whether it has opened a parenthesis, and no choice of probabilities changes that. Programming languages sit on two steps at once. Their syntax lives one step up: it is largely context-free, since matching nested brackets and blocks needs a stack, it is written in Backus–Naur form, and parsing it is decidable and fast. Their runtime behaviour, however, sits at the very top, since general-purpose languages are Turing complete. Yet each step adds structure, not meaning. A parser can tell you that `x = y + 1` is well formed, but not what `x` is for. What a program *means* is what it does, and Rice's theorem, which we meet in the next section, says that this cannot in general be read off its text.

Natural language is the mirror image: its meaning is rich, but its grammar resists formalization. Both worlds share one design decision: the symbol itself is atomic, an identity with no interior. `dawn` and `dusk` are as different to a parser as `dawn` and `xqzv`. Programmers know this: renaming every variable leaves the behavior of a program unchanged (alpha-equivalence). Natural language is the opposite: replacing one word by another in the same sentence changes what it says ("attack at dawn" is not "attack at dusk"), because each word carries meaning of its own. In a program, whatever meaning a human reads in `customer_balance` was smuggled in by the author. The machine only ever checks for equality not for meaning.

Linguistics offered only coarse ways out. A tag such as `NOUN` is the lowest-resolution embedding that could be built by hand, a class label that says almost nothing about the word. Parse trees and the Chomsky hierarchy are tree-shaped, a hint that hierarchies will need a geometry of their own (@sec-hyperbolic-spaces). The more radical way out was philosophical: the late Wittgenstein's "meaning is use" and Firth's "you shall know a word by the company it keeps" [@firth1957synopsis] move meaning from the symbol into its context. Statistics can measure context.

Anyone who has searched a database with ``WHERE content LIKE '%monarch%'`` and found no trace of "king" or "queen" has met this wall. Equality is the whole geometry of a symbol table, and the next section shows how poor that geometry is: written as one-hot vectors, every pair of distinct symbols sits at exactly the same distance, $\sqrt{2}$, so `dawn` is no closer to `dusk` than to `xqzv`. Giving symbols an interior, so that distance carries meaning, is what the rest of this chapter is about.

::: {.questions}
1. Write a program that decides whether a string of brackets `()[]{}` is balanced, using a stack.

2. Write a program that decides whether a string belongs to $\{a^n b^n c^n : n \ge 0\}$ (e.g., "aabbcc" belongs to the set, but "aaabbbcc" not) using no memory other than the input itself: a tape as long as the input, which you may overwrite, and a constant number of variables. Then try to adapt your stack-based solution of the previous question: what goes wrong?

3. Write an interpreter for MiniBrainf***, a tiny Turing-complete language. Its machine is a tape of cells, all starting at 0 and extending without limit to the right, with a head on the first cell. A program is a string of six instructions, executed in order: `>` and `<` move the head one cell right or left; `+` and `-` add or subtract 1 from the current cell; `.` prints the current cell; `[` jumps forward to the matching `]` if the current cell is 0; `]` jumps back to the matching `[` if the current cell is not 0. Run `++++++++[>++++++++<-]>+.`, then run `+[>+]` and `+[]` with a limit on the number of steps. Why can no linear-bounded automaton do what your interpreter does?
:::

## The Orthogonal Catastrophe: Why Symbolic Tables Hit a Geometric Wall

The Chomsky staircase has a hidden feature: it only climbs in one direction. Each step gives the machine more memory, from a bare state to a stack, a bounded tape and an unbounded tape, but all four steps rest on the same flat floor, the alphabet. A finite automaton decides what to do next by looking up its current state and the symbol it just read in a transition table. A pushdown automaton pushes and pops symbols and checks whether the top one is the one it expects. A Turing machine reads and writes symbols on its tape. In every case the only question a machine can ask about two symbols is whether they are the same. The staircase measures how much *structure* a machine can keep track of, and says nothing about how much *meaning* its symbols carry, because as far as the machine is concerned they carry none. We will call this the **orthogonal catastrophe**: a hierarchy of rich structure built on symbols that have no geometry, because, as we will see, every symbol sits at a right angle to every other and equally far from all of them.

To see the catastrophe we need to write symbols as numbers, since computers can only process numbers. The standard trick, known in machine learning jargon as **one-hot encoding**, is the following. Fix an ordering of the vocabulary $V$, a list of $|V|$ distinct symbols. The $j$-th symbol is represented by a vector with $|V|$ entries, all equal to 0 except for a single 1 in position $j$ (the "hot" entry). Take a toy vocabulary of five words:

| Word | Vector | $i=1$ | $i=2$ | $i=3$ | $i=4$ | $i=5$ |
|:---|:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| `dawn` | $\mathbf{e}_1$ | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `dusk` | $\mathbf{e}_2$ | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| `king` | $\mathbf{e}_3$ | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| `queen` | $\mathbf{e}_4$ | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| `xqzv` | $\mathbf{e}_5$ | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 |

: One-hot encoding of a five-word vocabulary. Each row is the vector $\mathbf{e}_j \in \mathbb{R}^5$ of a word, and the column $i$ gives its $i$-th entry, $(\mathbf{e}_j)_i = 1$ if $i = j$ and $0$ otherwise. {#tbl-one-hot}

A one-hot vector is just the position of a word in the vocabulary, written as a vector instead of as a number: the word is its index, and the index is the word, like the line number of an entry in a dictionary. It is also how the bottom step of the staircase looks in linear algebra. If the state of a finite automaton is written as a one-hot vector, reading a symbol is multiplying it by a matrix of zeros and ones that moves the single 1 to the next state. A probabilistic automaton uses a matrix of probabilities instead, and Shannon's bigram model is the same idea: multiplying a one-hot vector for the previous word by a table of next-word probabilities selects one row, the distribution of what comes next. In all these cases the one-hot vector acts as a pointer into a transition table, a matrix.

Multiplying by a matrix is one thing we can do with a one-hot vector; the other is to compare it with a second vector. The natural way to turn a pair of vectors into a single number is the **dot product**, $\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = \sum_k u_k v_k$: multiply the two vectors entry by entry and add the results. Each position in which both vectors are large contributes to the sum, so the dot product measures how much they have in common. Two vectors with dot product zero are **orthogonal**, which geometrically means that they form a right angle, and informally that they share nothing: no position is active in both. For one-hot vectors, the dot product with $\mathbf{e}_i$ selects the $i$-th entry of the other vector, $\langle \mathbf{e}_i, \mathbf{v} \rangle = v_i$, and when $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{e}_j$ that entry is 1 only if the two words are the same, so the dot product is a test for equality,

$$
\langle \mathbf{e}_i, \mathbf{e}_j \rangle = \delta_{ij} =
\begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } i = j, \\ 0 & \text{if } i \neq j, \end{cases}
$$

where $\delta_{ij}$ is the Kronecker delta. Distances follow immediately. Expanding the squared norm of the difference and using $\|\mathbf{e}_i\| = 1$,

$$
\|\mathbf{e}_i - \mathbf{e}_j\|_2^2 = \|\mathbf{e}_i\|^2 + \|\mathbf{e}_j\|^2 - 2\langle \mathbf{e}_i, \mathbf{e}_j \rangle = 1 + 1 - 0 = 2,
$$

so $\|\mathbf{e}_i - \mathbf{e}_j\|_2 = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$ for *every* pair of distinct words. In the toy vocabulary, `dawn` is exactly as far from `dusk` as from `xqzv`, and `king` is as far from `queen` as from `dawn`. The cosine similarity, which measures the angle, is 0 for every pair of distinct words as well. Whether we measure the distance between two words or their cosine similarity, the answer to "how similar are these two words?" is the same for all pairs, $\sqrt{2}$ in one case and 0 in the other, and therefore uninformative.

::: {.questions}
1. A finite automaton accepts the binary strings with an even number of 1s. Write its state as a one-hot vector of length 2 (even, odd) and give a $2 \times 2$ matrix to each input symbol, so that reading a symbol is a matrix–vector product. Check the result against the parity of the 1s on all strings of up to 10 symbols. What do the columns of these matrices look like, and how would they change for a probabilistic automaton?

2. Consider a logistic regression without bias, $p = \sigma(\langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{x} \rangle)$ with $\sigma(t) = 1/(1+e^{-t})$, trained on examples $(\mathbf{x}, y)$ with $y \in \{0, 1\}$ to minimize the cross-entropy loss $L = -y \ln p - (1-y)\ln(1-p)$. Derive the gradient $\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} L$ and write the gradient descent update of $\mathbf{w}$ with learning rate $\eta$. Which weights change when $\mathbf{x}$ is a one-hot vector? Then train the model to label `dawn` as 1 ("is a time of day") and `king` and `queen` as 0, twice: with one-hot inputs, and with the hand-made dense vectors of the table below, whose values are illustrative and not learned (`xqzv` gets a small noise vector). What probability does each model assign to `dusk`, which it never saw during training, and to `xqzv`?

   | Word | time of day | person | royal | male | brightness |
   |:---|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
   | `dawn` | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0.4 |
   | `dusk` | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 | $-0.4$ |
   | `king` | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0.5 | 0 |
   | `queen` | 0 | 1 | 1 | $-0.5$ | 0 |
   | `xqzv` | 0.2 | $-0.3$ | 0.1 | 0.3 | $-0.1$ |

3. Relabelling a vocabulary means permuting its words. Check that each of the $5! = 120$ relabellings of the one-hot vectors of @tbl-one-hot leaves the matrix of distances unchanged. Then exchange the labels `dawn` and `king` in the dense table of the previous question, so that each word receives the other's vector, and compare the distance between `dawn` and `dusk` before and after. What does the difference tell you about which of the two representations can contain meaning?
:::

One-hot vectors are equidistant, and equidistance is more than an inconvenience. It is the geometry of maximal ignorance, and it has four consequences, three of which the questions above probe.

- **There is no such thing as "nearby".** The nearest neighbours of `king` are all the other $|V|-1$ words, tied at distance $\sqrt{2}$. Retrieval, clustering and similarity search are all undefined. This is the `LIKE '%monarch%'` wall of the previous section.
- **Nothing transfers**. A linear model reading a one-hot vector computes $\langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{e}_i \rangle = w_i$: one independent parameter per word. Learning that "attack at dawn" is a military order tells it nothing about "attack at dusk", and a word that rarely appears gets a parameter that is barely trained.
- **The geometry is blind to renaming**. Permuting the coordinates, which is the same as relabelling the words, preserves every distance. This is the vector form of the alpha-equivalence we met for programs: renaming `customer_balance` to `x7` changes nothing. For a program that is a virtue. For language it is fatal, because exchanging `dawn` and `dusk` *does* change what a sentence says.
- **The dimension grows with the vocabulary.** A space of dimension $d$ contains at most $d$ mutually orthogonal non-zero vectors, so $|V|$ words forced to be orthogonal need $|V|$ dimensions. For a vocabulary of 50,000 words, each vector has 49,999 zeros and a single 1, and adding a new word changes the shape of the space.

The flaw lies in the encoding, not in the learner, which is why more data or a bigger model does not repair it. If similarity is to exist, it must be built into the representation itself: each word needs a position in a space whose geometry is not the trivial one, so that `dawn` can lie close to `dusk` and far from `xqzv`. The way out is surprisingly simple. Multiplying a one-hot vector by a matrix $\mathbf{E} \in \mathbb{R}^{|V| \times d}$ with $d \ll |V|$ just selects the $i$-th row, a dense vector of $d$ real numbers, and if the rows are learned instead of fixed, they are free to move closer together or farther apart. That matrix is an **embedding**, and the rest of this chapter and book will revolve around how embeddings work and where their values come from.

First, though, an objection. The catastrophe is a problem of symbols, and symbols have an advantage: for programs, their meaning can be pinned down with perfect formal precision. Perhaps we can repair the symbolic world from the inside, by defining exactly when two symbols or two programs *mean the same thing*, and skip the geometry altogether. The next section shows why this cannot work, and why the graded notion of similarity that an embedding provides is not a luxury but the only option left.

## Rice's Theorem: Why Exact Meaning Is Out of Reach

Symbols only support equality of *form*, and the equality we actually care about, *same meaning*, turns out to be out of reach even for programs, where meaning is perfectly formal.

Take two programs that sort a list, bubble sort and insertion sort. Their texts differ, so as symbols they are as far apart as `dawn` and `xqzv`: at distance $\sqrt{2}$, with nothing to say that they are siblings. Yet they compute the same function, and any user would call them the same program. This is equality of *meaning*, of what a program does rather than of how it is written, and it is exactly what Shannon left out by design and what the staircase does not measure. For natural language we can blame the vagueness of words. For programs we cannot, because the meaning of a program $M$ is a mathematical object, the partial function $\varphi_M$ that maps each input to the output of the program, or to nothing if it never halts. It looks as if we should be able to repair the symbolic world from the inside: write a procedure that decides when two programs have the same $\varphi$, and use it to group symbols by meaning. Rice's theorem says that no such procedure exists, and its proof uses the top step of the Chomsky staircase.

**Statement** [@rice1953classes]. A property $P$ of programs is *semantic* if it depends only on $\varphi_M$ and not on the text of $M$ (for example, "never outputs a negative number" or "computes the same function as program $N$"), and *non-trivial* if some programs have it and some do not. Then no algorithm decides, for every program $M$, whether $M$ has $P$. Syntactic properties such as "contains a `while` loop" stay decidable, which is why the parser of the Chomsky section works at all: it only reads the text.

**Proof sketch.** The ingredient is the halting problem [@turing1936computable]. We met it without naming it in the interpreter of the Chomsky exercises: with a step limit, `+[]` can only be abandoned, never declared endless, because a program that is still running might halt one step later. Turing proved that no algorithm settles halting for every program, and this is the extra power of the top step over a linear-bounded automaton, whose finitely many configurations make halting decidable. Now suppose a decider for $P$ exists. Without loss of generality, the program that loops forever does not have $P$ (otherwise decide the complement of $P$), and we can pick a program $Q$ that does. Given any program $M$ and input $x$, build $M'$ which, on input $y$, first runs $M$ on $x$ and, if that halts, then runs $Q$ on $y$. If $M$ halts on $x$, then $\varphi_{M'} = \varphi_Q$ and $M'$ has $P$; otherwise $M'$ loops forever on every input and does not. The decider would therefore solve the halting problem, which is impossible. In words: whatever you ask about the behaviour of a program, we can hide a halting question in front of that behaviour, so answering the first means answering the second.

**What it does not say.** Individual programs can often be analyzed. Type checkers, static analyzers and model checkers work by restricting the language, accepting false alarms, or giving up on some inputs. Running a program also settles some questions: if it halts within the budget, we see what it does. The theorem rules out a single method that is exact, general and always terminating. What survives is one-sided: we can confirm that a program has a property by finding it halting, but we cannot in general refute it.

**Why it matters here.** "Do these two programs mean the same thing?" and "Is this function safe?" cannot be answered exactly, so any practical notion of similar meaning for code has to be approximate and graded: a distance rather than an identity. This is what learned code embeddings provide [@alon2019code2vec]. They tend to place snippets with similar behaviour close together, with no guarantee. Embeddings do not escape Rice's theorem; they trade the impossible exact answer for a useful graded one. The same trade-off will reappear for words: there is no table of exact meanings to look up, only positions in a space from which similarity can be read. What remains is to see how such positions are obtained, starting with the idea that made them practical.

::: {.questions}
1. Use the interpreter of the previous exercises to write `prints_65(program, budget)` for the semantic property "halts and prints exactly 65". It runs the program for at most `budget` steps and returns `True` or `False` if the program halts within the budget, and `None` ("unknown") if the budget runs out. Test it on `++++++++[>++++++++<-]>+.`, on a program of 65 `+` followed by `.`, on `+.`, on `+[]` and `+[>+]`, and on a program of your own that prints 65 after a few thousand steps. How does the answer change when the budget grows? Which of the answers can never become a firm `False`, and what would it mean to get one for every program?

2. Represent a program as a Python generator function that yields once per step of computation and returns its result, and write `run(program, y, budget)` that steps it at most `budget` times and returns its result, or `None` if time runs out. Let $P$ be the property "returns 1 on input 0" and let $Q$ be a program that returns 1 at once. Write `build(M, x)`, which returns the program $M'$ of the proof sketch: on input $y$, run $M$ on $x$ and then $Q$ on $y$. Check that $M'$ has $P$ when $M$ is a program that halts after 100 steps, and that for $M$ = `while True: yield` no budget, however large, shows that $M'$ has $P$ or does not. Why does a decider for $P$ then solve the halting problem? Finally, why does the same construction not show that "contains a `while` loop" is undecidable?

3. Compare two ways of representing five programs: `bubble_sort`, `insertion_sort`, `sort_descending`, `identity` and `sort_unless_huge`, which sorts any list with fewer than 1,000 items and returns longer ones unchanged. In the first, each program is a symbol, a one-hot vector. In the second, it is the vector of its outputs on 30 random lists of 6 digits, concatenated. Compute the matrix of Euclidean distances for both representations. What does each say about `bubble_sort` and `insertion_sort`, and about `bubble_sort` and `sort_unless_huge`? Find an input that proves two of the programs different, and explain why a distance of zero between two programs proves nothing while a positive distance proves something. How does this connect to Rice's theorem?
:::

## Distributed Representations and Learned Manifolds

- **Distributed Representations:** Geoffrey Hinton's 1986 insight [@hinton1986learning]—distributing meaning across continuous dimensions where dot products measure semantic overlap.
- **Feature Engineering vs. Latent Manifolds:** Why handcrafted extrinsic features are brittle compared to self-supervised intrinsic manifolds.

## How Latent Spaces Are Born: The Four Generative Blueprints
*Four mathematical mechanisms convert raw unstructured data into continuous semantic manifolds:*

### Spectral & Distributional Factorization (SVD, PPMI, GloVe)
*Deriving low-rank coordinate systems from co-occurrence statistics.*
- Firth's distributional hypothesis [@firth1957synopsis] (*"You shall know a word by the company it keeps"*).
- Positive Pointwise Mutual Information (PPMI) and low-rank Eckart-Young approximation via SVD ($\mathbf{M} \approx \mathbf{U}_d \mathbf{\Sigma}_d \mathbf{V}_d^\top$).
- GloVe log-bilinear co-occurrence regression [@pennington2014glove].

### Predictive Push-Forwards (Word2Vec, Transformers)
*Optimizing local log-bilinear prediction and dynamic attention trajectories.*
- Word2Vec Skip-Gram with Negative Sampling (SGNS) and Levy & Goldberg's proof of implicit shifted-PMI factorization [@levy2014neural].
- Dynamic contextual latents in Transformers: token coordinates as trajectories through multi-head attention layers.

### Contrastive Metric Learning (InfoNCE, Triplet Loss)
*Pulling semantic neighbors together and repelling negatives on hyperspheres.*
- InfoNCE loss and temperature hyperparameter $\tau$ as a hard-negative mining dial.
- Wang & Isola's decomposition into *alignment* (pulling positive pairs) and *uniformity* (spreading points across the hypersphere $\mathbb{S}^{D-1}$) [@wang2020understanding].

### Probabilistic Manifolds (VAEs, Diffusion Latents)
*Enforcing continuous, gap-free semantic coverage via Gaussian priors and KL regularizers.*
- The failure of deterministic autoencoders (disconnected Dirac clusters and reconstruction voids).
- Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) and the KL divergence term as a geometric spring enforcing continuous manifold coverage.

## The Metric Geometry of Latent Space: Spheres, Angles, and Distances
*On unit hyperspheres, cosine similarity and Euclidean distance are monotonically linked, separating categorical direction ($\mathbf{z} / \|\mathbf{z}\|$) from salience/frequency ($\|\mathbf{z}\|$).*

- **Cosine vs. Euclidean Metrics:** Geometric equivalence on the unit hypersphere $\mathbb{S}^{D-1}$ ($\|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v}\|_2^2 = 2 - 2 \cos \theta$).
- **Direction vs. Magnitude:** Semantic angle encoding category/domain vs. vector norm encoding certainty, salience, and frequency.
- **Intrinsic vs. Extrinsic Dimensionality:** The Manifold Hypothesis ($d_{\text{int}} \ll D_{\text{ambient}}$).

## The Miracle of Vector Arithmetic: Linear Substructures of Thought
*Log-odds probability ratios map multiplicative linguistic relationships to additive vector translations ($\mathbf{king} - \mathbf{man} + \mathbf{woman} \approx \mathbf{queen}$) and LLM activation steering.*

- **The Analogical Parallelogram:** Mikolov's discovery of linear relational offsets [@mikolov2013efficient] ($\mathbf{v}_{\text{king}} - \mathbf{v}_{\text{man}} + \mathbf{v}_{\text{woman}} \approx \mathbf{v}_{\text{queen}}$).
- **Mathematical Origin:** Arora and Pennington's derivation showing how log-odds ratios in co-occurrences map multiplicative probabilities to linear displacements [@arora2016latent; @pennington2014glove].
- **Steering Vectors in Modern LLMs:** Activation addition in Transformer residual streams for model steering and safety.

## Pathologies of Flat Space: Anisotropy, Cones, and Hubness
*Unconstrained high-dimensional embeddings collapse into narrow eccentric cones with spurious nearest-neighbor hubs, requiring centering, whitening, and isotropic regularization.*

- **The Anisotropy Trap:** Dimensional collapse where all embeddings cluster inside a narrow eccentric cone ($\cos \theta \ge 0.85$).
- **The Hubness Phenomenon:** Spurious universal nearest neighbors in high-dimensional vector spaces.
- **Geometric Remedies:** Mean-centering, PCA whitening, and uniformity regularization.

## The Cracks in Flat Space: Exploration Hints and the Road Ahead
*The breakdown of flat Euclidean vector arithmetic reveals the structural limitations that motivate the rest of the book:*

- **$\rightarrow$ Chapter 2 (RAG & Vector DBs):** *Nearest-neighbor lookup cannot perform multi-hop reasoning or logical negation.*
- **$\rightarrow$ Chapter 3 (The High-Dimensional Trap):** *Orthogonal collapse and empty volumes in 1,536 dimensions.*
- **$\rightarrow$ Chapter 4 (Hyperbolic Spaces):** *Flat space cannot embed hierarchical taxonomies without exponential distortion.*
- **$\rightarrow$ Chapter 5 (Knowledge Graphs):** *Symmetric dot products fail on asymmetric and typed relations, requiring complex rotations (RotatE).*
- **$\rightarrow$ Chapter 6 (Topological Deep Learning):** *Pairwise distances miss multi-way interactions and topological holes.*
- **$\rightarrow$ Chapter 7 (Complex & Quantum Latents):** *Non-commutative reasoning and phase interference in $\mathbb{C}^D$.*
- **$\rightarrow$ Chapter 8 (Vector Symbolic Architectures):** *Exact variable binding ($\circledast$) and bundling without neural retraining.*
- **$\rightarrow$ Chapter 9 (Neurosymbolic AI):** *Tensor Product Representations and emergent compositional syntax.*
- **$\rightarrow$ Chapter 10 (Optimal Transport):** *Aligning disconnected multimodal manifolds with Wasserstein geometry.*

## Further Reading {.unnumbered}

The four generative blueprints surveyed here are not unrelated techniques but convergent
estimators of the same underlying co-occurrence statistic; @arora2016latent develops the
latent-variable argument for why PMI-based factorization and log-bilinear regression
agree, and @levy2014neural shows the predictive Word2Vec objective is itself an implicit
factorization of a shifted-PMI matrix — readers wanting the full derivation of the
log-bilinear GloVe objective should consult @pennington2014glove directly. The next
chapter's argument about embedding dimensionality rests on the Johnson–Lindenstrauss
lemma [@johnson1984extensions, pp. 189-206], which bounds how much a point set can be
projected into lower dimensions while approximately preserving pairwise distances.
